justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a relatively stable near-term outlook with a mild upward drift over longer horizons. For the one-day estimate, I anchored closely to the prevailing market price, assuming that intraday momentum and overnight positioning would keep the asset in a tight range without a major catalyst to shift direction. The one-week estimate nudges slightly higher, reflecting a modest continuation of whatever underlying trend appeared intact at the time of the forecast, while the one-month estimate drifts a bit further upward, incorporating a small risk premium and the assumption that any near-term consolidation would eventually resolve in the direction of the prevailing trend. In all three cases, the point estimates are relatively close together, signaling my view that this asset was not in a period of rapid directional movement.

The confidence interval widths expand naturally as the time horizon lengthens, which reflects the compounding uncertainty that comes with more time for new information to arrive. At one day, the interval is narrow because the main drivers are technical in nature — overnight gaps, liquidity conditions, and short-term sentiment — all of which tend to be mean-reverting within a small range. By one week, macro data releases, central bank commentary, or shifts in risk appetite can meaningfully move prices, so the interval widens to account for those possibilities. At one month, the range becomes quite wide because a full calendar month contains numerous scheduled and unscheduled events capable of repricing the asset significantly in either direction.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside my stated intervals. On the upside, a surprise positive catalyst — such as a stronger-than-expected economic report, a policy announcement, or a sudden surge in institutional demand — could drive prices well above the upper bound of even the one-month interval. On the downside, a sharp deterioration in broader market sentiment, a geopolitical shock, or a liquidity event could send prices below the lower bound of my confidence intervals at any horizon. The one-day interval is particularly vulnerable to gap risk from overnight news, which by definition cannot be fully anticipated in a symmetric distribution.

It is also worth noting that my confidence intervals assume roughly log-normal return distributions, which tend to underweight fat-tail events. Real markets exhibit heavier tails than a normal distribution implies, meaning that extreme outcomes — both positive and negative — occur more frequently than my stated 90% interval would suggest. Traders and risk managers relying on this forecast should treat the interval bounds as probabilistic guideposts rather than hard limits, and should consider scenario analysis around tail events that my model may not fully capture.
